abstract: The world`s arid regions are home to diverse assemblages of small mammals, many of which possess a range of physiological, behavioral, and sensory adaptations to the harsh selective pressures imposed by arid environments. The mammalian skull facilitates a range of sensory functions, meaning that arid-dwelling species likely possess distinct skull adaptations which have evolved in response to the unique selective pressures imposed by arid environments. Studies on arid-adapted rodents have highlighted hearing as being important for arid adaptation; however, the adaptive potential of the entire skull is rarely considered. Here, we used 3D geometric morphometrics to test for signatures of arid adaptation using 168 skulls across 30 species of the Sminthopsinae, a subfamily of small insectivorous marsupials, found across Australia. We found that relative bulla size increased by 20% along an aridity gradient from mesic to hyper arid. We also found that species further from the equator tended to have wider posterior nasal cavities, which may be related to selection for thermoregulatory capabilities. Our findings demonstrate the role of the skull in facilitating adaptation to aridity and provide further evidence that selection for improved low-frequency hearing appears to be a key driver of skull shape in arid-zone small mammals.
